title: Statements and Arguments — Strong vs Weak
tagline: Year 3 — Judging arguments for and against a proposal: relevance, importance, specificity and practicality

introduction.overview: In a statement-and-argument question you are given a proposal (usually "Should X be done?") and two arguments. You do not decide whether the proposal is right; you decide whether each argument is strong or weak. A strong argument is important, directly related to the proposal and based on facts or sound reasoning. A weak argument is vague, trivial, based on personal likes, or only loosely related.
introduction.placementRelevance: Argument-strength questions are a regular part of logical-reasoning sections in company tests.
introduction.realWorldContext: Weighing the reasons offered in a meeting, a debate or a policy note uses the same judgement.

learningObjectives: Apply the four tests: relevant, important, specific, practical
Spot weak arguments based on imitation, taste or exaggeration
Accept arguments for and against that are both strong
Use the four standard answer options correctly

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: A strong argument supports or opposes the statement with a real, relevant reason. A weak argument gives a trivial, personal or irrelevant reason.

coreDefinitions: Strong argument: relevant to the statement, important in size, and based on facts or sound reasoning.
Weak argument: vague, trivial, emotional, based on personal taste, or about a different issue.
Imitation argument: "other countries do it" is weak unless it gives the reason it works.
Exaggeration: words such as "only way", "never" or "everyone" usually make an argument weak.
Opposite sides: an argument for and an argument against can both be strong.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Ask: if this reason were true, would it seriously matter for a sensible decision on the proposal? If yes, it is strong.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Test each argument on four questions: Is it about this proposal? Is it important? Is it specific? Does it avoid exaggeration? A "no" to the first two makes it weak.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Importance test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Is the effect large or serious?

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Specificity test
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: It pollutes vs it is bad

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Pair rule
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: For and against can both be strong

mainNarrative: Statement: Should plastic bags be banned? Argument I says yes because they pollute the environment and harm animals. This is relevant, important and specific, so it is strong. Argument II says no because they are cheap. Cheapness is a minor point compared with environmental harm, so it is weak.

Imitation is a common weak argument. "The government should give free vaccines because other countries do" gives no reason. "Because it prevents serious diseases and protects the community" gives the reason and is strong.

Both arguments can be strong when they take opposite sides on real grounds. Should cash be replaced entirely by digital payments? "Digital payments are faster and traceable" is strong; "many villages lack internet and smartphones" is also strong.
Exaggeration weakens an argument. "Exams are the only way to ever know anything" overstates; "exams cause some students stress" is true but too small a reason to abolish them. Neither is strong.

For decisions with extreme actions, such as banning all imports, check whether the argument addresses the extreme: a reason such as "key inputs are not produced domestically" directly shows why the extreme step is unwise.

deepDiveAspects.title: Personal taste
deepDiveAspects.content: "Students will not like it" or "people enjoy driving" describe preferences, not consequences.

deepDiveAspects.title: Possibility vs probability
deepDiveAspects.content: "Some employees may misuse it" is a bare possibility and is usually weak unless backed by evidence.

solvedExamples.title: Strong versus weak
solvedExamples.question: Should smoking be banned in public places? I. Yes, passive smoke harms the health of non-smokers. II. No, smokers will feel unhappy. Which is strong?

steps.title: Argument I
steps.explanation: Health harm to others is relevant and important: strong.

steps.title: Argument II
steps.explanation: Unhappiness of smokers is minor next to health risk: weak.

solvedExamples.title: Both strong
solvedExamples.question: Should the retirement age be raised to 65? I. Yes, people live longer and stay productive. II. No, it will reduce job openings for young people. Which is strong?

steps.title: Argument I
steps.explanation: Longevity and productivity are relevant facts: strong.

steps.title: Argument II
steps.explanation: Fewer openings for the young is a real effect: strong.

solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Opposite arguments can both be strong.

solvedExamples.title: Neither strong
solvedExamples.question: Should students be given pocket money? I. Yes, because everyone should have some money. II. No, because it is bad. Which is strong?

steps.title: Argument I
steps.explanation: "Everyone should" is a vague claim: weak.

steps.title: Argument II
steps.explanation: "It is bad" gives no reason: weak.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: Neither argument I nor II is strong
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: Neither names a concrete benefit or harm.

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Check relevance, importance, specificity and exaggeration for each argument separately; ignore which side you favour.

commonMistakes.howToAvoid: Check the link to the proposal.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: If both arguments are vague, the answer is neither.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Mark absolute words and personal-taste words.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Strong arguments name a concrete benefit or harm.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I reject an imitation argument?
Can I accept two opposite strong arguments?
